title: NURS 1021 Unit 1 Case Study 5
description: 24-year-old male with severe aplastic anemia after benzene solvent exposure: pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), febrile neutropenia, neutropenic and bleeding precautions, antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporine.

authorReview.note: New case written by Claude on 25 Nov 2026 (NURS 1021 Unit 1, batch 2); checked against Merck Manual Professional (Aplastic Anemia, Mar 2025). Please review: irradiated/leukoreduced products and avoiding family-donor blood (standard hematology practice, not on the Merck page); excluding flowers and plants (agency policies vary); ATG infusion details (premedication, in-line filter, at least 4 hours) against the product monograph and your agency.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Select the 4 findings that require follow-up.

options.text: Petechiae on both lower legs and unexplained bruises
Liver and spleen not palpable
Takes no regular medications
No enlarged lymph nodes
Lungs clear on auscultation
Temperature of 38.6° C with chills
Heart rate of 118 beats/min with shortness of breath on stairs
Nosebleed lasting 40 minutes and bleeding gums

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: fever with chills may be the first sign of a serious infection when white cells are low (Option 6). Prolonged nosebleeds, bleeding gums (Option 8), petechiae and unexplained bruising (Option 1) point to a low platelet count. Tachycardia with exertional dyspnea and pallor reflect anemia: the heart beats faster to deliver oxygen with less hemoglobin (Option 7). Together, signs of anemia, infection and bleeding suggest that all three cell lines are low (pancytopenia), the picture of bone marrow failure.

Do not require follow-up: the absence of enlarged lymph nodes, liver and spleen is a helpful negative: aplastic anemia does not enlarge the spleen, whereas leukemia and lymphoma often enlarge nodes, liver or spleen (Options 2 and 4). Taking no medications (Option 3) and clear lungs (Option 5) need no action; medication and chemical exposures are still recorded as possible causes.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is mainly caused by anemia, neutropenia, or thrombocytopenia.

rows.text: Tiredness and shortness of breath on exertion
Painful mouth ulcers and sore throat
Bleeding gums and a prolonged nosebleed

question.explanation:
Why all three: in aplastic anemia the hematopoietic stem cells are lost, usually through an immune attack that may be triggered by a toxin (benzene), a drug, radiation or a virus. The marrow becomes empty and fatty, so it makes too few red cells, white cells and platelets. His results show severe disease: neutrophils 0.3 × 10⁹/L, platelets 9 × 10⁹/L and absolute reticulocytes 12 × 10⁹/L. The smear has no blasts (unlike leukemia), and the PT and aPTT are normal (unlike DIC).

Anemia: less hemoglobin means less oxygen delivery: fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, pallor and tachycardia. The low reticulocyte count shows the marrow is not responding.

Neutropenia: without neutrophils, bacteria and fungi invade mucous membranes, causing mouth ulcers, sore throat and fever. Infections can be life-threatening, and the usual signs (pus, swelling) may be absent.

Thrombocytopenia: platelets form the first plug in small vessels; when they are very low, the client has petechiae, bruising and mucosal bleeding (gums, nose).

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: Kevin's results are most consistent with [[drop0]]. The most likely cause is [[drop1]]. The nurse's priority is [[drop2]].

options.text: iron deficiency anemia
acute leukemia
severe aplastic anemia
disseminated intravascular coagulation
an enlarged spleen trapping blood cells
repeated skin contact with a benzene solvent
an inherited deficiency of factor VIII
a diet low in iron and folate
activity intolerance from anemia
a spontaneous bleed from the low platelet count
sepsis from fever with a very low neutrophil count
anxiety about the diagnosis

question.explanation:
Severe aplastic anemia: pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow (about 10%, replaced by fat) and no abnormal cells. It is severe because cellularity is below 25% and at least two of these are present: neutrophils below 0.5 × 10⁹/L, absolute reticulocytes below 60 × 10⁹/L, platelets below 20 × 10⁹/L. Leukemia fills the marrow with blasts; DIC prolongs the PT and aPTT.

Cause: benzene is a well-known marrow toxin, absorbed through the skin and lungs; about half of cases have no cause found. Diet causes deficiency anemias, not pancytopenia with an empty marrow; aplastic anemia does not enlarge the spleen.

Priority: fever with neutrophils below 0.5 × 10⁹/L is febrile neutropenia, a medical emergency: infection can progress to septic shock within hours, and his heart rate is rising and BP falling. Blood cultures are drawn and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are started within 60 minutes. Bleeding risk is high and is managed with precautions and platelets, but untreated sepsis is the more immediate threat to life.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 1 1700 and the Orders.
question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in Kevin's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Provide a soft toothbrush or foam swabs and an electric razor
Keep fresh flowers and potted plants out of the room
Arrange for his brother to donate platelets for him
Check his temperature every 4 hours and report 38.0° C or higher at once
Give ibuprofen for his mouth pain
Check that every blood product is labelled irradiated and leukoreduced
Perform hand hygiene before and after every contact with Kevin
Give a glycerin suppository if he becomes constipated

question.explanation:
Include: hand hygiene is the most effective way to prevent infection in a neutropenic client (Option 7). Fever may be the only sign of infection when neutrophils are absent, so it is reported at once (Option 4). Soft brushes, swabs and electric razors prevent bleeding from gums and skin (Option 1). Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in clients receiving antithymocyte globulin, and leukoreduction lowers the risk of sensitization to donor cells and of cytomegalovirus transmission (Option 6). Flowers, plants and standing water can carry bacteria and fungi such as Aspergillus (Option 2).

Do not include: suppositories, enemas and rectal temperatures can injure the rectal mucosa, causing bleeding and a portal for bacteria (Option 8). Blood from relatives is avoided in clients who may need a stem cell transplant, because it can sensitize them to a family donor's tissue antigens (Option 3). NSAIDs inhibit platelet function (Option 5).

question.stem: For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated for the first ATG infusion.

rows.text: Give the prescribed premedications (acetaminophen, an antihistamine and a corticosteroid) before the infusion
Give the ATG as a rapid IV push to shorten the time he is exposed to it
Infuse the ATG through an in-line filter over at least 4 hours
Keep epinephrine and resuscitation equipment at the bedside
Weigh Kevin before each dose of ATG
Stop the infusion and call for help if he develops wheezing, hypotension or throat tightness

question.explanation:
Indicated: ATG is an animal (horse) antibody against human T cells; it removes the T cells that attack the stem cells. Because it is a foreign protein, infusion reactions (fever, chills, rash) and anaphylaxis can occur, so premedication is given, the infusion runs slowly through an in-line filter over at least 4 hours, emergency drugs and equipment are at hand, and the infusion is stopped at the first sign of anaphylaxis. Serum sickness (fever, rash, joint pain) can follow 1 to 2 weeks later.

Contraindicated: a rapid IV push greatly increases the risk of a severe reaction.

Non-Essential: the ATG dose is calculated from his weight on admission; weighing before each daily dose adds nothing to safety.

question.stem: For each statement Kevin makes, click to specify whether it shows that the teaching was understood or that he needs further teaching.

rows.text: “I'll go to the emergency department if my temperature is 38.0° C or higher.”
“My counts are coming up, so I can stop the cyclosporine once I feel well.”
“I'll keep my blood tests and check my blood pressure, because cyclosporine can affect my kidneys and blood pressure.”
“I'll go back to cleaning parts with the solvent, but I'll wear gloves.”
“I'll avoid grapefruit and check with the pharmacist before taking any new medicine.”
“It may take several months for my blood counts to recover.”

question.explanation:
Response so far: neutrophils (0.3 to 1.1 × 10⁹/L), platelets (9 to 38 × 10⁹/L) and reticulocytes are rising and he needs fewer transfusions: a partial response. About 60% to 70% of clients respond to ATG and cyclosporine, usually over 3 to 6 months, so treatment continues.

Understood: fever is still an emergency while neutrophils are low. Cyclosporine is nephrotoxic and raises blood pressure (134/86 mm Hg today), so creatinine, cyclosporine levels and BP are checked. Grapefruit and many drugs raise cyclosporine levels. Recovery takes months.

Needs further teaching: stopping cyclosporine early risks relapse; it is tapered only on the hematologist's instruction. Benzene is a marrow toxin absorbed through the skin and by inhalation; gloves alone do not remove the exposure, so he should not return to that work and should discuss it with occupational health.
